options.why: As a reference study written for the U.S. government, the excerpt reports incentives, slogans and enrollment and birth figures but gives no individual Korean voices.

options.text: It was written before the South Korean government had begun any family planning programs
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The study was completed in 1990 and describes policies that began in the 1960s and continued through the 1980s.

options.text: It was produced by South Korean officials seeking to promote the program to other Asian states
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The context line says the book was written for the U.S. government; foreign officials training in Seoul are mentioned only as evidence of the program's success.

options.text: It discusses only rural villages and leaves out urban centers such as Seoul and Pusan
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt deals with national policies and statistics and names Seoul; nothing limits it to rural areas.

facts: South Korea's family planning programs began in the 1960s.
The Library of Congress Country Studies series was produced for the U.S. government.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt consists of government measures and aggregate figures, such as school enrollment and births per couple, written by U.S. government researchers, with no testimony from families.
design.evidence_quote: the number of middle school students alone dropped by half a million during the 1980s

items.stem: EXTRA. South Korea's decision to admit more foreign workers around 1990, as described in the excerpt, is best understood as part of which broader process?

options.text: Rising migration of workers from poorer states to wealthier industrial economies
options.label: key
options.why: In the late twentieth century labor migrants moved in growing numbers from less developed countries to richer economies, and South Korea's labor shortage made it one of those destinations.

options.text: The nineteenth-century system of indentured labor that moved South Asian workers to plantation colonies
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Indentured migration to plantation colonies belongs to the era of nineteenth-century imperialism, not to the globalized economy of 1990.

options.text: Refugee movements produced by the partition of British India into India and Pakistan in 1947
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Partition caused huge forced movements tied to decolonization, not economic migration into an industrializing East Asian state.

options.text: The free movement of workers among member states guaranteed by the European Union
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Free movement of labor is a European regional arrangement and does not apply to South Korea.

facts: Labor migration from developing countries to wealthier economies increased in the late twentieth century as part of globalization.
The partition of British India took place in 1947.
Indentured labor from South Asia went to plantation colonies such as Trinidad and Fiji in the nineteenth century.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt reports the authorization of foreign workers and factories hiring illegal immigrants, signs that South Korea was becoming a destination for labor migrants.
design.evidence_quote: Many factories already had been compensating for such shortfalls by hiring illegal immigrants (1,000 such workers were deported in 1990)

items.stem: The painting, made around 1581 for the Ottoman court, was most likely created to serve which purpose?

options.text: To glorify Murad III's reign by showing the court's patronage of learning
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says the work was made for the Ottoman court and shows an observatory the sultan ordered built. Court-sponsored illustrated histories like the Sehinsahname celebrated the sultan's reign, and patronage of scholarship added to his prestige.

options.text: To teach European navigators how to use Ottoman astrolabes and quadrants on ocean voyages
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the image, credit line or context points to a European or nautical audience. The work was made for the Ottoman court.

options.text: To record the religious scholars' arguments for closing the observatory as un-Islamic
options.label: reversal
options.why: The painting celebrates the scholars at work. It does not record the opposition that led to the observatory's demolition in 1580.

options.text: To announce that Ottoman astronomers had adopted the Copernican sun-centered model
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: No cosmological model is shown or stated. Taqi al-Din's work belonged to the Islamic observational tradition and did not promote heliocentrism.

facts: Sultan Murad III supported the founding of Taqi al-Din's observatory in Istanbul in the mid-1570s.
The Sehinsahname is an illustrated court history of Murad III's reign produced in the late sixteenth century.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line states the painting was made for the Ottoman court and shows the observatory Murad III ordered built.
design.evidence_quote: made around 1581 for the Ottoman court and shows astronomers at the Istanbul observatory that Sultan Murad III had ordered built

items.stem: Which claim about the pursuit of knowledge at the Ottoman court does the painting most directly convey?

options.text: It was produced by teams of scholars measuring the sky with precise instruments
options.label: key
options.why: The image shows many turbaned scholars working together with astrolabes, quadrants, an hourglass, a clock and large measuring rods. This presents astronomy as organized, cooperative observation.

options.text: It depended mainly on telescopes and other instruments recently imported from western Europe
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: No telescope appears, since the telescope was not invented until 1608. The instruments shown belong to the long-standing Islamic astronomical tradition.

options.text: It was reserved for the sultan alone, who personally carried out the observations
options.label: reversal
options.why: The painting shows a large group of scholars doing the work, not the sultan observing by himself.

options.text: It served chiefly to forecast the outcome of military campaigns against the Habsburgs
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: No military or Habsburg subject appears in the image, so the source gives no support for this purpose.

facts: The telescope was first developed in the Netherlands around 1608.
Astrolabes and quadrants were standard instruments of Islamic astronomy long before the sixteenth century.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Many scholars are shown working together with astrolabes, quadrants, an hourglass, a clock and large measuring instruments.

items.stem: The founding of the observatory shown in the painting is best understood in the context of which broader development of the period c. 1450 to c. 1750?

options.text: Rulers of land-based empires funding art, architecture, and science to display power
options.label: key
options.why: Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal rulers paid for monuments, painting workshops and scholarship to legitimize their rule. The sultan's observatory and the court painting that records it both fit this pattern.

options.text: The spread of Enlightenment salons and learned scientific societies through the major Ottoman cities
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Enlightenment salons were mainly a European development of the eighteenth century. They came long after a 1570s observatory and did not shape it.

options.text: Ottoman territorial losses in the Balkans after the Treaty of Karlowitz forced reforms
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Treaty of Karlowitz dates from 1699, more than a century after the observatory was founded.

options.text: Sufi missionaries spreading Islam along Indian Ocean trade routes into Southeast Asia
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This was a real development, but it has nothing to do with court-sponsored astronomy in Istanbul.

facts: Land-based empires such as the Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals used monumental architecture and court arts to legitimize rule in the sixteenth century.
The Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) ceded Ottoman territory in central Europe, including most of Hungary, to the Habsburgs.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line ties the observatory to Sultan Murad III's order, and the painting was made for the court, which shows imperial patronage.
design.evidence_quote: the Istanbul observatory that Sultan Murad III had ordered built around 1575

items.stem: Which of the following developments in another land-based empire of the period c. 1450 to c. 1750 was most similar to the project shown in the painting?

options.text: Jai Singh II's building of large observatories in Mughal-ruled India in the 1700s
options.label: key
options.why: Jai Singh II, a Rajput ruler serving the Mughals, built large observatories at Delhi, Jaipur and other cities in the early 1700s. Like the Istanbul observatory, these were elite-sponsored centers for measuring the heavens.

options.text: The Yongzheng emperor's ban on Christian missionary activity in Qing China in the 1720s
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This was a restriction on religious activity, not the sponsorship of an astronomical institution.

options.text: The Tokugawa shogunate's limits on European trade to the Dutch at Nagasaki after the 1630s
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This was a policy on foreign trade and contact, not state patronage of observational science.

options.text: The Safavid shah Ismail's imposition of Twelver Shia Islam as Iran's official faith
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This was a real use of state power in a land-based empire, but it concerned religion, not scientific patronage.

facts: Jai Singh II built astronomical observatories (Jantar Mantar) at Delhi and Jaipur in the 1720s and 1730s.
Shah Ismail I made Twelver Shia Islam the official religion of Safavid Iran after 1501.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The painting shows an observatory with scholars using astronomical instruments, which students compare with another empire's observatories.
design.evidence_quote: shows astronomers at the Istanbul observatory

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following most limits the painting's usefulness as evidence of how Ottoman society as a whole viewed the observatory?

options.text: As a court work, it celebrates the project and omits the critics who had it torn down
options.label: key
options.why: Because the painting was made for the court, it shows the observatory in a favorable light. It leaves out the opposition from religious figures that led to the observatory's demolition in 1580.

options.text: It was painted by a European visitor who had never seen Ottoman scientific instruments
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line identifies the artist as a court painter working for the Ottoman court.

options.text: It was painted more than a century after the observatory closed and relied on hearsay accounts
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The work dates to about 1581, only a few years after the observatory was founded and just after it was demolished.

options.text: It depicts only foreign Christian scholars and leaves out the observatory's Muslim astronomers
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the source identifies the turbaned scholars as foreign Christians. The context line calls them Ottoman astronomers.

facts: The Istanbul observatory of Taqi al-Din was demolished in 1580 after opposition at court and among religious figures.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line names a court painter, and the context line says the work was made for the Ottoman court, so it reflects the court's favorable view.
design.evidence_quote: This painting was made around 1581 for the Ottoman court

items.stem: EXTRA: Which feature of the painting best supports the claim that the observatory's work joined instrument observation with written scholarship?

options.text: Book-filled cabinets and men writing at desks beside the instruments
options.label: key
options.why: The painting shows cabinets stacked with books and several scholars writing or reading near the astrolabes and quadrants. This links observation to recorded learning.

options.text: A sultan enthroned at the center of the room, personally directing each astronomer
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: No enthroned sultan appears in the painting. The figures shown are scholars and an attendant.

options.text: A window opening onto a harbor crowded with Ottoman galleys and merchant ships
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The painting shows only the observatory's interior, with no harbor or ships.

options.text: Janissary soldiers with muskets standing guard over the instruments at the doorway
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: No armed soldiers are shown. The only standing figure apart from the scholars is an unarmed attendant.

facts: Islamic observatories, including those at Maragha (1259) and Samarkand (1420s), combined instrument observation with the compilation of written astronomical tables.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Visible cabinets of books at the upper right and scholars writing on paper at the lower left appear alongside the instruments.

items.stem: In the decade between the 1910 and 1920 figures in the table, which development killed tens of millions of people worldwide without reversing long-term population growth?

options.text: The influenza pandemic of 1918 to 1919
options.label: key
options.why: The 1918 to 1919 influenza pandemic killed tens of millions worldwide, yet world population was still larger in 1920 than in 1910 and kept growing afterward.

options.text: The spread of bubonic plague across Afro-Eurasia trade routes
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Black Death struck Afro-Eurasia in the mid-1300s, centuries before this table begins.

options.text: The famine caused by the collectivization policies of the Great Leap Forward
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Leap Forward famine happened in China from 1959 to 1961, after the last year in the table.

options.text: The Soviet famine in Ukraine that followed forced collectivization
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The famine in Ukraine (the Holodomor) took place in 1932 to 1933, not in the 1910s.

facts: The influenza pandemic of 1918 to 1919 killed tens of millions of people worldwide.
The Great Leap Forward famine took place in China from 1959 to 1961.
The Soviet famine in Ukraine happened in 1932 to 1933.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The table covers 1910 and 1920, and its estimates show world population was higher in 1920 even though the pandemic struck between those years.
design.evidence_quote: Estimated world population, 1900-1950

items.stem: The data in the table would best support which of the following claims about the first half of the twentieth century?

options.text: World population grew substantially even though two world wars took place.
options.label: key
options.why: Both the lower and upper estimates for 1950 are well above those for 1900, so the population kept growing through the wars of 1914 to 1918 and 1939 to 1945.

options.text: Deaths in the two world wars caused world population to shrink between 1900 and 1950.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The table shows the opposite: estimates for 1950 are much higher than estimates for 1900.

options.text: World population more than doubled between 1900 and 1950 because birth rates rose so quickly.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The estimates rise by roughly half, not by more than double. The table also gives no birth rates.

options.text: Most of the world's population growth between 1900 and 1950 took place in South and East Asia.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table gives only world totals, with no regional breakdown, so it cannot support a claim about where the growth happened.

facts: World War I lasted from 1914 to 1918 and World War II from 1939 to 1945.
World population is estimated to have grown from roughly 1.6 to 1.7 billion in 1900 to roughly 2.5 billion in 1950.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The 1950 lower and upper estimates are both well above the 1900 estimates, even though the period includes both world wars.
design.evidence_quote: summary lower and upper estimates, millions

items.stem: The overall trend shown in the table is best explained in the context of which broader development of the period?

options.text: Falling death rates as public health measures and medicine spread
options.label: key
options.why: Sanitation, vaccination, better medical knowledge, and by the 1940s antibiotics such as penicillin lowered death rates. Population grew because fewer people died, while birth rates stayed high in many regions.

options.text: Large harvest gains from high-yield seeds and chemical fertilizers of the Green Revolution
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Green Revolution spread mainly from the 1960s on, after the period the table covers.

options.text: Fertility in most industrialized societies falling below the level needed to replace each generation
options.label: reversal
options.why: Fertility below replacement level is a late twentieth century trend that slows population growth. It does not explain the growth shown here.

options.text: Higher living standards across Africa and Asia that followed the end of European colonial rule
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Most decolonization happened after 1945, mainly after 1950, so it cannot explain growth that began in 1900.

facts: Penicillin became widely used in the 1940s.
The Green Revolution in agriculture spread mainly from the 1960s.
Most African and Asian colonies gained independence after 1945.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The estimates rise steadily from 1900 to 1950, which fits a period when death rates were falling.
design.evidence_quote: Estimated world population, 1900-1950

items.stem: Which of the following developments in the second half of the twentieth century most directly continued the trend shown in the table?

options.text: Population growth sped up, and the world passed 6 billion by about 2000.
options.label: key
options.why: After 1950, growth sped up rather than slowing. World population passed about 6 billion around 2000, continuing the rise shown in the table.

options.text: World population fell after 1950 as industrialized countries adopted family planning programs.
options.label: reversal
options.why: World population did not fall after 1950. It rose faster than before, even where birth rates declined.

options.text: World population stopped growing after China's one-child policy reduced births across Asia.
options.label: overstated
options.why: China's one-child policy began in 1979 and slowed growth in China, but world population kept rising quickly.

options.text: Europe's share of world population grew as postwar baby booms spread across the continent.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Europe's share of world population fell after 1950 because Asia, Africa, and Latin America grew much faster.

facts: World population reached about 6 billion around 1999 to 2000.
China's one-child policy was introduced in 1979.
Europe's share of world population declined in the late twentieth century.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The table shows a rising trend from 1900 to 1950, which students connect to faster growth later in the century.
design.evidence_quote: Estimated world population, 1900-1950

items.stem: Which of the following is the most important limitation of the table for a historian studying population change from 1900 to 1950?

options.text: Its figures are scholars' estimates that differ, not exact counts.
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says the table shows the lowest and highest of several scholars' estimates. Many regions had no reliable census in this period, so the figures are reconstructions with real uncertainty.

options.text: A United States government agency compiled it, so it probably inflates figures to serve wartime propaganda.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the credit or context line suggests propaganda. The table was compiled from scholarly estimates published from 1974 to 1999, long after the wars.

options.text: It leaves out people living in colonies because colonial subjects were not counted in world totals.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The source presents world population estimates. Nothing indicates that colonized populations were excluded.

options.text: It covers only the years of the two world wars, so it cannot show peacetime trends in population.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table gives figures for 1900 through 1950 by decade, including peacetime years such as 1900, 1910, 1920, and 1930.

facts: Many regions of the world lacked reliable national censuses in the early twentieth century.
The Census Bureau table compiles published estimates by several scholars and the United Nations.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line explains that the table shows the lowest and highest of estimates made by several scholars.
design.evidence_quote: this table shows the lowest and highest of those estimates for six years

items.stem: Population growth like that in the table was connected to which development of the 1930s that contributed to the causes of World War II?

options.text: Japan's leaders citing a need for land and resources to justify seizing Manchuria in 1931
options.label: key
options.why: Japanese leaders pointed to population pressure and a lack of resources at home to justify expansion into Manchuria in 1931, one of the aggressive acts that led toward World War II.

options.text: Overcrowding in European cities that directly set off the alliance crisis of 1914 after the Sarajevo assassination
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The 1914 crisis led to World War I, not World War II. It grew out of nationalism, militarism, and alliances, not overcrowding.

options.text: Population pressure in Latin America leading its governments to launch wars of conquest in Africa
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Latin American states did not conquer territory in Africa. Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935.

options.text: Collapsing birth rates in Germany that caused the Nazis to reject any expansion beyond its borders
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Nazi regime pursued expansion in search of 'living space' in eastern Europe. It did not reject expansion.

facts: Japan seized Manchuria after the Mukden Incident in 1931.
Japanese leaders cited population pressure and resource needs to justify expansion.
Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The steady rise in world population in the table links to arguments by expansionist states in the 1930s about population pressure and resources.
design.evidence_quote: Estimated world population, 1900-1950

items.stem: Marco Polo calls the tree-lined highways "the greatest possible solace to travellers." His praise most likely reflects his point of view as

options.text: a merchant whose own journeys depended on well-marked and secure overland routes
options.label: key
options.why: The context line identifies Polo as a Venetian merchant who spent years in Mongol China. A long-distance traveler would especially value marked roads where "no one can miss the way."

options.text: a Chinese scholar-official praising Confucian ideals of benevolent rule to win promotion through the exams
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Polo was a Venetian outsider, not a Chinese official taking the examinations.

options.text: a Christian missionary sent by the pope to convert the Khan and to build churches in Dadu
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The context line calls Polo a merchant, not a missionary, and the excerpt says nothing about religious conversion.

options.text: a Mongol general responsible for building military roads during the conquest of the Song
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Polo was a foreign visitor, not a Mongol commander, and the passage presents the roads as a help to messengers and ordinary travelers.

facts: Marco Polo was a Venetian merchant who traveled to Yuan China and stayed there for years in the late 1200s.
Kublai Khan ruled the Yuan dynasty, which he proclaimed in 1271.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line calls Polo a Venetian merchant, and the text stresses that the trees comfort travelers and keep them from losing the way.
design.evidence_quote: it is the greatest possible solace to travellers

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Polo's main claim in the first part of the excerpt?

options.text: The Khan's government routinely relieved subjects struck by natural disasters.
options.label: key
options.why: Polo says the emperor checks for dearth caused by storms or locusts, cancels taxes, and supplies grain and cattle, helping the people "every year."

options.text: Mongol rule caused repeated famines by imposing crushing taxes on Chinese peasant farmers.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Polo says the opposite: people hit by disaster pay no taxes that year.

options.text: Local officials, rather than the emperor, paid for disaster relief out of their private estates.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Polo says the grain is the emperor's own ('corn of his own'). Officials only report conditions.

options.text: Most of the empire's grain was exported along the Silk Roads, leaving provinces short of seed.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt does not mention grain exports. Shortages are blamed on bad seasons, storms and locusts.

facts: The Yuan state, like earlier Chinese dynasties, gave tax remissions and grain relief in times of famine.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The first segment describes tax remission, grain for food and seed, and gifts of cattle to people hurt by calamities.
design.evidence_quote: the Lord every year helps and fosters the people subject to him

items.stem: Polo's description of highways marked for the emperor's messengers is best understood in the context of which broader development of the thirteenth century?

options.text: Mongol rulers maintained relay stations and roads that made Eurasian travel safer.
options.label: key
options.why: The Mongol yam courier system and the security of the Pax Mongolica eased the movement of messengers, merchants and travelers like Polo across Eurasia.

options.text: Song rulers spread fast-ripening Champa rice, which raised harvests across southern China.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Song did promote Champa rice, but that is about farming, not the roads and messengers the excerpt describes.

options.text: Ming emperors sponsored Zheng He's voyages, which carried tribute missions across the Indian Ocean.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Zheng He's voyages (1405 to 1433) came after the Yuan had fallen, and they were sea voyages, not overland roads.

options.text: Camel caravans organized by Mali's rulers linked West African gold fields to Mediterranean ports.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Trans-Saharan trade was a real network of exchange, but it is not the context for road policy in Yuan China.

facts: The Mongol Empire ran the yam, a network of relay stations for official messengers, in the 1200s.
Mongol control across Eurasia in the 1200s and 1300s made Silk Road travel safer (the Pax Mongolica).

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt says the highways were 'travelled by his messengers' and were marked even through uninhabited land, which fits the Mongol relay and road system.
design.evidence_quote: all the highways travelled by his messengers and the people generally should be planted with rows of great trees

items.stem: Kublai's relief policies described in the excerpt most directly illustrate which pattern in Mongol rule over China?

options.text: Mongol rulers kept older Chinese state practices for managing grain and taxes.
options.label: key
options.why: Yuan rulers kept much of the Chinese administrative system. Officials reported harvest conditions, and the state cancelled taxes and handed out grain, as earlier dynasties had done.

options.text: Mongol rulers made the civil service exams the main path to office for Chinese scholars.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Yuan held no civil service exams until 1315 and limited Chinese scholars' access to high office.

options.text: Mongol rulers in China converted to Islam and adopted sharia as the basis of law.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This describes the Ilkhanate in Persia under Ghazan, not Yuan China.

options.text: Mongol rulers abolished Chinese bureaucracy and governed through nomadic clan councils alone.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt shows the Khan relying on officials across his provinces. The Yuan kept a bureaucratic state.

facts: The Yuan dynasty kept much of the Chinese bureaucratic system while reserving top posts mainly for Mongols and other non-Chinese.
The Yuan did not hold civil service examinations until 1315.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The Khan sends messengers to 'his officers' to check for dearth and then cancels taxes and supplies grain, which matches Chinese bureaucratic relief practice.
design.evidence_quote: to ascertain from his officers if the people are afflicted by any dearth

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following most limits the usefulness of the excerpt as evidence of how Yuan famine relief actually worked across the empire?

options.text: Polo was an admiring outsider who may have overstated how uniform the policies were.
options.label: key
options.why: Polo calls the relief 'a great bounty' and says the trees line 'all the ways.' Such sweeping praise from a foreign visitor may not show how consistently the policies were carried out.

options.text: Polo wrote in Chinese for Yuan officials, so he repeated official propaganda word for word.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The credit line says the account was dictated to Rusticiano da Pisa. Nothing shows it was written in Chinese for Yuan officials.

options.text: Polo never left Venice and based the whole account on rumors he heard from Arab traders in port.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The context line says Polo spent years in Mongol-ruled China.

options.text: Polo described only the period after the Yuan collapse, when Ming rulers had reformed the relief system.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The account dates to about 1298 and describes Kublai's rule. The Yuan fell in 1368.

facts: Polo's account was dictated to Rusticiano da Pisa around 1298.
The Yuan dynasty fell in 1368 and was replaced by the Ming.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Polo's words of praise ('undoubtedly a great bounty') and sweeping claims ('all the ways') show an admiring and generalizing point of view.
design.evidence_quote: Now this is undoubtedly a great bounty on his part.

items.stem: EXTRA. Accounts such as Polo's, describing the wealth and order of Yuan China, had which effect in Europe in later centuries?

options.text: They raised European interest in Asian wealth and in new routes to reach Asia.
options.label: key
options.why: Polo's account was widely copied and read in Europe. It fed curiosity about Asia's riches, and later explorers such as Columbus read it.

options.text: They persuaded the Yuan court to adopt Latin Christianity as the official faith of China.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The Yuan never adopted Latin Christianity, and Polo's account was read in Europe, not at the Yuan court.

options.text: They led European states to found the Hanseatic League to trade directly with Chinese ports.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Hanseatic League was a trading network of northern European towns centered on the Baltic and North Seas. It had nothing to do with China.

options.text: They convinced Italian city-states to give up Mediterranean trade with the Mamluks and Byzantines.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Venice and Genoa kept trading heavily in the eastern Mediterranean after Polo's time.

facts: Marco Polo's account circulated widely in manuscript in Europe after about 1298.
Christopher Columbus owned and annotated a copy of Polo's book.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt's picture of a rich, well-run empire with generous rulers and well-marked roads is the kind of description that drew European interest in Asia.

items.stem: Livingstone's point of view in the excerpt was most likely shaped by which of the following?

options.text: Antislavery and missionary convictions that commerce and Christianity could transform African societies
options.label: key
options.why: Livingstone was a Scottish missionary writing as British abolitionism peaked. He proposes trade as a way to make the slave trade impossible, which matches the belief that commerce and Christianity together would reform Africa.

options.text: Portuguese colonial interest in enlarging coastal slave exports from Angola and Mozambique to supply plantation labor in Brazil
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt aims to end the slave trade, not expand it, and Livingstone was a British subject, not a Portuguese official.

options.text: Mercantilist convictions that colonies should trade only with the home country through chartered monopoly companies
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt says nothing about restricting trade to a mother country or using monopoly companies. By the 1850s Britain had largely turned to free trade.

options.text: Socialist critiques arguing that industrial capitalism exploited wage laborers in European factories and mines
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Socialist ideas did exist by the 1850s, but the excerpt praises trade in European manufactured goods instead of criticizing industrial capitalism.

facts: Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most of its empire through the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833.
Livingstone was a Scottish missionary who promoted commerce and Christianity as remedies for the slave trade in the 1850s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line identifies Livingstone as a missionary, and the text proposes legitimate commerce as a way to end the slave trade.
design.evidence_quote: if the slave-market were supplied with articles of European manufacture by legitimate commerce, the trade in slaves would become impossible

items.stem: Which of the following developments in nineteenth-century Africa would best support Livingstone's argument that legitimate commerce could replace the slave trade?

options.text: After Atlantic slave exports were suppressed, Niger Delta traders shifted to selling palm oil to British industry
options.label: key
options.why: West African merchants moved from exporting captives to exporting palm oil for British industry. This is a case of trade in products taking the place of slave exports, which is what Livingstone predicts.

options.text: During the mid-1800s, slave exports from East Africa through Zanzibar expanded at the same time as ivory exports grew
options.label: reversal
options.why: Here the ivory trade and the slave trade grew together, which would weaken Livingstone's claim that trading ivory would prevent slave trading.

options.text: Enslaved people in the southern United States grew most of the raw cotton that supplied textile mills of Lancashire in northern England
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate, but it concerns slave labor feeding British industry in the Americas. It shows nothing about African trade in goods replacing the sale of captives.

options.text: Demand for sugar in Europe drove a sharp increase in the number of Africans shipped across the Atlantic after 1750
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This shows rising demand for slaves. It does not show that trade in other goods could replace the slave trade.

facts: In the nineteenth century, palm oil exports from West Africa, including the Niger Delta, grew to supply British industry as the Atlantic slave trade declined.
The East African slave trade through Zanzibar expanded in the nineteenth century.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Livingstone argues that exchanging European goods for African products would stop the slave trade at its beginning, so a real case of goods replacing captives as exports would support him.
design.evidence_quote: in exchange for ivory and other products of the country, and thus prevent the trade at the beginning

items.stem: Which of the following was an important context for Livingstone's 1857 proposal to end the slave trade in Africa?

options.text: Britain had banned the slave trade in 1807 and used naval patrols to suppress it
options.label: key
options.why: British abolition of the slave trade and naval suppression efforts explain why a British missionary in the 1850s was looking for ways to stop the trade at its source.

options.text: The Berlin Conference had set rules for European powers claiming territory across the African continent
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Berlin Conference met in 1884 and 1885, almost thirty years after this book was published.

options.text: Zulu expansion under Shaka had displaced many peoples across southern Africa in the early nineteenth century
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is a real southern African development, but it does not explain a proposal to use European trade goods to end the slave trade.

options.text: The Haitian Revolution had abolished slavery and created an independent state in the Caribbean
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is accurate, but it concerns the Caribbean, not the British antislavery campaign aimed at African trade that Livingstone addresses.

facts: Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807, and the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron worked to suppress it.
The Berlin Conference met in 1884 and 1885.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The 1857 date and the goal of making the slave trade impossible point to the British abolitionist campaign already underway.
design.evidence_quote: than to try to put a stop to it at any of the subsequent steps

items.stem: Livingstone's call for a highway from the coast into the center of Africa is most directly related to which later development of the late 1800s?

options.text: Growing European interest in the interior that fed the Scramble for Africa
options.label: key
options.why: Explorers' accounts of the interior and calls for routes inland increased European interest in the region. This helped lead to the Scramble for Africa and the colonization of the interior in the 1880s and 1890s.

options.text: The rapid end of all slavery within African societies once inland trade routes opened
options.label: overstated
options.why: Slavery and slave trading inside Africa lasted well past the 1800s, so opening trade did not quickly end them.

options.text: The French-financed construction of the Suez Canal to link the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Suez Canal (1869) was a sea route between oceans built by a French-led company. It had nothing to do with a road from the African coast inland.

options.text: The Boxer Rebellion against foreign missionaries and traders in northern China
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Boxer Rebellion (1899 to 1901) was a response to foreign influence in China and has no connection to opening Africa's interior.

facts: The Scramble for Africa brought most of Africa under European colonial rule between about 1880 and 1914.
Livingstone's travels and writings in the 1850s raised British public interest in central Africa.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Livingstone's call for a route from the coast to the center of the country anticipates the European push into the interior later in the century.
design.evidence_quote: This could only be effected by establishing a highway from the coast into the centre of the country.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains the concept of legitimate commerce as Livingstone uses the term in the excerpt?

options.text: Trade in African products such as ivory and palm oil promoted as a substitute for selling captives
options.label: key
options.why: Livingstone uses legitimate commerce to mean exchanging European goods for products like ivory, as opposed to trade in people. Abolitionists promoted this kind of trade as a way to replace the slave trade.

options.text: Indenture contracts that moved Indian and Chinese laborers to plantations in the Caribbean after emancipation
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Indentured labor migration was a real development after emancipation, but it involved moving workers, not trading in African products.

options.text: Free-trade policies such as Britain's 1846 repeal of the Corn Laws, which lowered tariffs on grain imported into Britain
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Corn Laws were repealed in 1846, but that was a British tariff policy and not the African trade in products that Livingstone describes.

options.text: Unequal treaties that forced Qing China to open ports to British merchants selling opium
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The unequal treaties are an example of economic imperialism in East Asia and have nothing to do with replacing the African slave trade.

facts: In the nineteenth century, abolitionists used the term legitimate commerce for trade in goods such as palm oil and ivory, as opposed to trade in enslaved people.
Britain repealed the Corn Laws in 1846.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt sets legitimate commerce, meaning exchange for ivory and other products, against the trade in slaves.
design.evidence_quote: by legitimate commerce, the trade in slaves would become impossible

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main claim Livingstone makes in the excerpt?

options.text: Trading European goods for African products would remove the incentive to sell people
options.label: key
options.why: Livingstone argues that if people could get European goods in exchange for ivory and other products, they would no longer sell captives for them.

options.text: Naval patrols intercepting slave ships off the coast offered the surest way to end the trade in captives
options.label: reversal
options.why: Livingstone says it is more practical to stop the trade at its beginning than at the later steps, where patrols at sea would act.

options.text: African societies should be placed under direct European colonial rule before slavery could end
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt proposes trade and a road inland. It does not call for European political control.

options.text: European manufactured goods should be kept out of Africa because they fuel slave markets
options.label: reversal
options.why: Livingstone wants more European goods supplied through legitimate trade, not fewer.

facts: In the mid-1800s, British abolitionists debated whether naval suppression or the promotion of trade would better end the African slave trade.
Livingstone promoted commerce as a remedy for the slave trade in the 1850s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Livingstone says exchanging goods for ivory and other products would stop the trade at its beginning rather than at a later step.
design.evidence_quote: It seemed more feasible to give the goods, for which the people now part with their servants, in exchange for ivory

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the historical situation in which the photograph was taken?

options.text: Superpower rivalry in which the United States and the Soviet Union competed for prestige through space exploration
options.label: key
options.why: The credit line identifies a NASA astronaut on Apollo 8 in December 1968, during the Cold War Space Race between the United States and the Soviet Union.

options.text: The years after the Soviet Union collapsed, when the United States led international scientific cooperation in orbit
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, more than twenty years after this 1968 photograph.

options.text: The Second World War, when German engineers developed V-2 rockets, the first human-made objects to cross into outer space
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: V-2 rockets belong to the 1940s. The photograph dates from 1968, during the Cold War.

options.text: A period of joint Soviet and American missions designed to end the arms race by sharing rocket technology between the rival blocs
options.label: reversal
options.why: In 1968 the superpowers were competing in space, not cooperating, and they did not share rocket technology to end the arms race.

facts: Apollo 8 was the first crewed mission to orbit the Moon, in December 1968.
The United States and the Soviet Union competed in a Space Race during the Cold War.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line and context line date the photograph to December 1968 and identify it as the work of a NASA astronaut on Apollo 8.
design.evidence_quote: William Anders, NASA astronaut (U.S. government photograph), 1968 (December 24).

items.stem: As a visual statement, the photograph most directly conveys which of the following ideas?

options.text: Earth is a single, small, and isolated world, with no visible national borders dividing it
options.label: key
options.why: The image shows Earth as one bright sphere alone in black space above a barren lunar horizon, with no political divisions visible.

options.text: The Moon is a valuable frontier whose mineral resources could support future human colonies and industry
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The lunar surface appears empty and cratered. Nothing in the image suggests resources or settlement.

options.text: The United States had achieved permanent military superiority over the Soviet Union in outer space
options.label: overstated
options.why: The image contains no military content, and no power held permanent superiority in space.

options.text: Human industry has already scarred the planet, as shown by visible pollution spreading across the continents
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: From lunar distance the photograph shows clouds and landforms. No pollution can be seen.

facts: Apollo 8 photographed Earth from lunar orbit in December 1968.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The composition sets a lone Earth, with no visible borders, against black space above the lifeless lunar surface.

items.stem: In the years after 1968, this photograph was widely reproduced as an environmental symbol. That use is best understood in the context of which broader development?

options.text: Growing international concern about pollution, shown by the first Earth Day in 1970 and the 1972 Stockholm conference
options.label: key
options.why: The image of a single, finite Earth circulated just as environmental movements expanded, with Earth Day in 1970 and the UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm in 1972.

options.text: The spread of Green Revolution farming methods, which raised grain yields in Asia and Latin America through fertilizers and new seeds
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Green Revolution was a real change in agriculture, but it does not explain why the photograph became an environmental symbol.

options.text: The wave of decolonization in Africa, during which new states such as Ghana and Kenya gained independence from British imperial rule
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Decolonization was a major process of the period, but it is not connected to the photograph's use as an environmental image.

options.text: The detente era arms control talks, in which the superpowers agreed to limit strategic nuclear weapons through the SALT I treaty
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: SALT I (1972) was about nuclear weapons, not environmental awareness.

facts: The first Earth Day was held in 1970.
The UN Conference on the Human Environment met in Stockholm in 1972.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The 1968 date places the image just before the major environmental milestones of the early 1970s.
design.evidence_quote: The crew of Apollo 8 took this photograph in December 1968 while orbiting the Moon.

items.stem: The environmental awareness that the photograph later came to symbolize most directly contributed to which of the following later developments?

options.text: International agreements such as the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, which set targets for cutting greenhouse gas emissions
options.label: key
options.why: Growing global environmental concern after the late 1960s led to international climate agreements such as the Kyoto Protocol in 1997.

options.text: The founding of the United Nations in 1945 to preserve peace and to promote cooperation among sovereign states after World War II
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The UN was founded in 1945, decades before this 1968 photograph, so it cannot have resulted from awareness the image inspired.

options.text: The Green Revolution of the 1960s, which expanded the use of chemical fertilizers, pesticides, and irrigation in developing countries
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Green Revolution started before 1968 and increased chemical use. It was not a result of environmental awareness.

options.text: The Non-Aligned Movement, which brought together newly independent states seeking to avoid alignment with either Cold War bloc
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Non-Aligned Movement (founded in 1961) was about Cold War politics, not the environment.

facts: The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in 1997 to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
The Non-Aligned Movement was founded in 1961.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The image of a lone, finite Earth relates to later international efforts to protect the planet as a whole.

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following earlier developments most directly prompted the United States to expand the space program that produced this photograph?

options.text: The Soviet launch of Sputnik in 1957, the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth
options.label: key
options.why: Sputnik's launch in 1957 alarmed American leaders and led to the creation of NASA in 1958 and to the space program that included Apollo 8.

options.text: The Korean War, which led the United States to commit troops to defend South Korea against a northern invasion
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Korean War (1950-1953) was a Cold War conflict, but it did not drive the expansion of the American space program.

options.text: The Marshall Plan, through which the United States funded the economic rebuilding of Western European nations
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Marshall Plan was economic aid for Europe and had nothing to do with space exploration.

options.text: The Soviet Union's collapse in 1991, which left the United States as the sole superpower able to fund space missions
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The collapse came in 1991, long after the 1968 Apollo 8 mission.

facts: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, in 1957.
NASA was created in 1958.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line identifies the photographer as a NASA astronaut, which links the image to the American space program that grew in response to Soviet achievements.
design.evidence_quote: William Anders, NASA astronaut (U.S. government photograph)

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following is a limitation of the photograph as evidence for the rise of global environmental awareness?

options.text: It shows the view from lunar orbit but not how viewers around the world responded to it
options.label: key
options.why: The image records what the crew saw. It cannot show how audiences reacted to it or how it shaped environmental movements, which historians must document with other sources.

options.text: It was taken by a Soviet cosmonaut and therefore reflects only the perspective of the communist bloc
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line identifies the photographer as a NASA astronaut on an American mission.

options.text: It was produced decades after environmental movements had already achieved their major international treaties
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The photograph dates from 1968, before Stockholm (1972) and Kyoto (1997).

options.text: It shows Earth's continents in such detail that viewers could identify the boundaries of individual nations
options.label: reversal
options.why: From lunar distance no national borders are visible. Earth appears as one undivided sphere.

facts: Apollo 8 was a United States NASA mission in 1968.
The Stockholm environmental conference took place in 1972.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The photograph shows only the view from lunar orbit and gives no information about how people received it.
design.evidence_quote: The crew of Apollo 8 took this photograph in December 1968 while orbiting the Moon.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a main idea shared by Source A and Source B?

options.text: Both present a Japanese tradition as the product of gradual development over a long period.
options.label: key
options.why: Okakura traces tea from medicine to beverage to Tang poetry to fifteenth-century Teaism. Nitobe calls bushido an organic growth of decades and centuries with no single fountain head.

options.text: Both argue that the traditions were borrowed from China and preserved in Japan without any significant change.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Okakura says Japan transformed tea into Teaism, and Nitobe never mentions China. Neither author describes a tradition kept unchanged.

options.text: Both trace the traditions to formal written codes issued by Japanese rulers to regulate the behavior of the elite.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Nitobe stresses that bushido is unwritten and that the Buke Hatto barely dealt with ethics. Okakura names no code at all.

options.text: Both claim that the traditions were open to all social classes rather than being limited to elites.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Okakura's talk of Eastern democracy is a figure of speech about taste, and Nitobe describes a code meant only for the knights, the warrior class.

facts: Lu Yu's Classic of Tea was written in Tang China in the eighth century.
The Japanese tea ceremony took shape in the fifteenth century under the Ashikaga (Muromachi) shogunate.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Okakura lays out tea's history in stages across centuries, and Nitobe says bushido has no single founder or starting point.
design.evidence_quote: It was an organic growth of decades and centuries of military career.

items.stem: Nitobe's references in Source B to the English Constitution, the Magna Charta, and the Norman Conquest most likely served to

options.text: make Japanese feudal history easier for Western readers to understand through familiar parallels
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says Nitobe wrote in English to explain the warrior code to Western readers. Comparing bushido with English institutions gives those readers a familiar reference point.

options.text: argue that Japan's government should replace its feudal customs with a written British-style constitution
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nitobe describes and explains bushido. He proposes no political reform, and Meiji Japan had already ended the feudal order before 1900.

options.text: show that Japanese feudal institutions were originally copied from models brought by English merchants
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Nitobe draws a parallel, not a line of descent. He dates Japanese feudalism to Yoritomo, which rules out any English origin.

options.text: criticize British imperial expansion in Asia by showing that Japan's institutions were older than England's
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt says nothing about empire, and it actually dates English feudalism (from 1066) earlier than Japan's (late twelfth century).

facts: Japan's Meiji government abolished the feudal domains in 1871 and issued a written constitution in 1889.
The Norman Conquest of England took place in 1066.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the book was written for Western readers, and the text keeps pairing Japanese history with English examples.
design.evidence_quote: As in England the political institutions of feudalism may be said to date from the Norman Conquest

items.stem: The rise of feudalism that Nitobe ties to the ascendency of Yoritomo late in the twelfth century took place in the context of

options.text: the rise of a shogunate in which warrior leaders held power while emperors remained largely ceremonial
options.label: key
options.why: Minamoto no Yoritomo founded the Kamakura shogunate. Real power passed to the shogun and his warrior vassals, while the imperial court in Kyoto kept mostly ceremonial authority.

options.text: the unification of Japan under Tokugawa shoguns after more than a century of warfare among rival regional lords
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Tokugawa unification happened around 1600. That is four centuries after Yoritomo and outside this unit.

options.text: the adoption of a centralized Chinese-style bureaucracy in which the emperor ruled through appointed scholar-officials
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Chinese-style reforms date to the seventh century. Yoritomo's rise moved Japan away from imperial central rule, not toward it.

options.text: the Mongol conquest of Japan, which placed the islands under the authority of the Yuan dynasty ruling from Beijing
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 failed. Japan was never conquered, and the attacks came about a century after Yoritomo.

facts: Minamoto no Yoritomo won the Genpei War in 1185 and received the title of shogun in 1192, founding the Kamakura shogunate.
Mongol invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281 failed.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Nitobe dates the rise of Japanese feudalism to Yoritomo's ascendency in the late twelfth century, which is when the Kamakura shogunate was founded.
design.evidence_quote: in Japan its rise was simultaneous with the ascendency of Yoritomo, late in the twelfth century.

items.stem: The movement of tea culture from China to Japan described in Source A was most closely connected to which development in the period c. 1200 to c. 1450?

options.text: Japanese Buddhist monks who studied in China brought back Zen teachings and tea-drinking customs
options.label: key
options.why: Monks such as Eisai studied in Song China and brought Chan (Zen) Buddhism and tea practices back to Japan. Zen temples then helped shape the tea culture that Okakura says Japan ennobled.

options.text: Portuguese merchants carried Chinese tea to Japanese ports as part of their expanding Indian Ocean trade network
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Portuguese did not reach Japan until the 1540s, long after tea culture was established there.

options.text: Mongol rulers of the Yuan dynasty imposed Chinese customs on Japan after incorporating it into their empire
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Yuan never conquered Japan, so they could not have imposed customs on it.

options.text: Muslim merchants traveling the Silk Roads introduced tea to Japan as part of the spread of Sufi devotional practice
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Sufism spread through Muslim trade networks in Central, South, and Southeast Asia. It played no part in bringing tea to Japan.

facts: The Japanese monk Eisai brought Rinzai Zen from Song China to Japan in 1191 and wrote a treatise promoting tea in 1211.
Portuguese traders first reached Japan in the 1540s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Okakura places early tea culture in China and its fifteenth-century transformation in Japan, which points to cultural transmission between the two.
design.evidence_quote: The fifteenth century saw Japan ennoble it into a religion of aestheticism--Teaism.

items.stem: Which of the following would most directly challenge Okakura's claim in Source A about the long isolation of Japan during the period c. 1200 to c. 1450?

options.text: Ashikaga shoguns took part in official tribute trade with Ming China in the early 1400s
options.label: key
options.why: Formal tributary trade with the Ming shows ongoing official contact with China in the same century Okakura credits with Teaism. That undercuts his claim that isolation shaped it.

options.text: Kamakura warriors built defensive stone walls along the coast of Kyushu to keep foreign invaders from landing
options.label: reversal
options.why: Coastal defenses against the Mongols fit an image of a Japan guarding its borders. They would support Okakura's claim of isolation, not challenge it.

options.text: Tokugawa shoguns restricted European trade to a small Dutch post at Nagasaki beginning in the 1630s and 1640s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Tokugawa trade limits came two centuries after the fifteenth century and would seem to support the isolation claim anyway.

options.text: Japanese court writers composed poetry and prose in a native phonetic script instead of only in Chinese characters
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Native script shows Japan's cultural distinctiveness. It says nothing about whether Japan was cut off from other societies.

facts: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu entered a tributary trade relationship with Ming China in the early 1400s.
After the 1274 Mongol invasion, Kamakura Japan built a stone defensive wall along Hakata Bay in Kyushu.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Okakura says Japan's long isolation favoured Teaism, which he dates to the fifteenth century, the same century as the Ming tribute trade.
design.evidence_quote: The long isolation of Japan from the rest of the world, so conducive to introspection, has been highly favourable to the development of Teaism.

items.stem: The warrior code Nitobe describes in Source B is most similar to which development in another region in the period c. 1200 to c. 1450?

options.text: Ideals of chivalry shaped the expected conduct of knights who served lords in western Europe
options.label: key
options.why: Like bushido, chivalry set ideals of loyalty and behavior for a hereditary warrior elite within a feudal order. Nitobe himself compares Japan with English feudalism.

options.text: Scholar-officials chosen through civil service exams staffed the bureaucracy of the Song dynasty in China
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Song China was run by an exam-selected civilian elite. That is a contrast to Japan's warrior-led feudal order, not a parallel.

options.text: Islamic jurists in Dar al-Islam developed systems of law based on the Quran and hadith to guide all believers
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Islamic law was a written scholarly tradition meant for all believers. Nitobe describes an unwritten code for one warrior class.

options.text: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca displayed the wealth of Mali and spread its fame across the Mediterranean world
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The pilgrimage was a real event of the period, but it concerns Islam and trade wealth, not a code of conduct for warriors.

facts: Codes of chivalry shaped the ideals of European knights in the High and Late Middle Ages.
Mansa Musa of Mali made his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Nitobe calls the samurai knights and compares Japanese feudalism with English feudalism, which points to a European parallel.
design.evidence_quote: Bushido, then, is the code of moral principles which the knights were required or instructed to observe.

items.stem: Humboldt's point of view in the excerpt was most directly shaped by which of the following?

options.text: Enlightenment science that sought general natural laws through observation and comparison
options.label: key
options.why: Humboldt corrects an older theory of how trees affect springs. He then calls his three connected phenomena a general rule and supports it with cases from Lombardy and Lower Peru. That is the empirical, comparative method of Enlightenment natural science.

options.text: His duties as a Spanish colonial official charged with raising royal revenue from the plantations of Aragua
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The context line calls Humboldt a Prussian naturalist traveling in Spanish colonies. He was not a Spanish official, and the excerpt says nothing about royal revenue.

options.text: His support for creole revolutionaries who blamed Spanish rule for the economic decline of Venezuela
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt blames European planters' land clearing for environmental damage. It makes no political argument about Spanish rule or independence, and it describes growing cultivation, not economic decline.

options.text: Romantic criticism of the coal-burning factories then spreading across Prussian cities
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Large-scale factory industry in Prussia came after 1800. The excerpt is about plantation agriculture and forests, not factories.

facts: Alexander von Humboldt traveled in Spanish America from 1799 to 1804 as a scientific observer.
Enlightenment natural science stressed empirical observation and the search for general laws of nature.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Humboldt rejects what 'was long believed' and backs up a general rule with evidence from regions in both hemispheres.
design.evidence_quote: Countries situated in opposite hemispheres, as, for example, Lombardy bordered by the Alps, and Lower Peru

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main claim Humboldt makes in the excerpt?

options.text: Clearing forested slopes both dries up springs and produces sudden, destructive floods
options.label: key
options.why: Humboldt says felling trees brings scarcity of water. He describes torrents and destructive inundations, then calls forest clearing, lost springs, and torrents 'closely connected.'

options.text: Trees supply springs mainly because their leaves attract water vapor that is spread through the air
options.label: reversal
options.why: Humboldt rejects this explicitly. He says trees affect springs 'not, as was long believed' through attracting vapors, but by shading the soil and reducing evaporation.

options.text: Deforestation damages water supplies only in tropical colonies, unlike temperate lands such as Lombardy
options.label: reversal
options.why: Humboldt says the damage happens 'in every climate.' He uses Lombardy as supporting evidence, not as a counterexample.

options.text: Indigenous farmers caused the lake to shrink by draining its waters for irrigation
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt blames European planters and the spread of sugar, indigo, and cotton cultivation. It does not blame Indigenous irrigation.

facts: Humboldt studied the shrinking Lake Valencia in the Aragua valleys of Venezuela in 1800.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Humboldt sums up his argument in the sentence linking forest clearing, the loss of permanent springs, and torrents.
design.evidence_quote: the clearing of forests, the want of permanent springs, and the existence of torrents, are three phenomena closely connected together

items.stem: The expansion of sugar, indigo, and cotton in the valleys of Aragua after the mid-1700s is best understood in the context of which development?

options.text: Bourbon reforms that expanded trade within the Spanish empire and promoted colonial exports
options.label: key
options.why: In the later 1700s, Spain's Bourbon reforms loosened trade restrictions within the empire and encouraged colonies to produce exports. This fits Humboldt's timeline: forests stood until the mid-1700s and then gave way to cash crops.

options.text: Independence wars that broke up the great estates and handed their land to formerly enslaved soldiers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Venezuela's independence wars began after 1810, so they could not explain changes Humboldt saw in 1800. Large estates also largely survived independence.

options.text: Railroads built with British capital that linked the interior valleys of Venezuela to Caribbean ports
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Railroads built with British investment in Latin America belong to the later nineteenth century, long after the changes described.

options.text: The abolition of slavery in Spanish America, which freed labor for new plantation crops
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Venezuela abolished slavery in 1854, decades after 1800. Plantation expansion before 1800 relied on slavery rather than following its end.

facts: The Spanish Bourbon reforms of the eighteenth century included freer trade within the empire, such as the comercio libre decree of 1778.
Venezuela abolished slavery in 1854.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Humboldt dates the forest cover to the middle of the eighteenth century and ties its loss to growing cultivation of export crops.
design.evidence_quote: With the destruction of the trees, and the increase of the cultivation of sugar, indigo, and cotton

items.stem: The changes in land use Humboldt describes are most similar to which development elsewhere in the nineteenth century?

options.text: The spread of cotton growing for export in Egypt under Muhammad Ali
options.label: key
options.why: In both cases, land was turned over to cash crops for export markets. Humboldt shows Aragua shifting to sugar, indigo, and cotton, and Muhammad Ali pushed long-staple cotton for export in Egypt.

options.text: The Meiji government's building of state-owned silk-reeling and munitions factories in Japan
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This was state-led industrialization, not the conversion of land to export agriculture that the excerpt describes.

options.text: The Russian emancipation of the serfs in 1861, which ended landlords' legal control over peasants
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Emancipation was a legal change in labor status. It did not mean clearing land for export cash crops.

options.text: The Qing restriction of European merchants to the single port of Canton
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Canton system was a trade policy and had nothing to do with converting forest or land to plantation crops.

facts: Muhammad Ali, ruler of Egypt from 1805 to 1848, promoted long-staple cotton cultivation for export starting in the 1820s.
The Meiji government built state-run model factories in the 1870s, and Russia emancipated its serfs in 1861.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt shows forest and brushwood replaced by sugar, indigo, and cotton grown for market.
design.evidence_quote: the increase of the cultivation of sugar, indigo, and cotton

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following is a limitation of the excerpt for historians studying the plantation economy of Aragua around 1800?

options.text: It gives a visiting scientist's view and omits the views of those who worked the estates
options.label: key
options.why: Humboldt was a traveling foreign naturalist who focused on forests, springs, and the lake. The excerpt records nothing from the enslaved and free laborers who did the plantation work.

options.text: It was written by a Spanish crown official and so conceals royal responsibility for clearing forests
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The context line identifies Humboldt as a Prussian naturalist, not a Spanish official.

options.text: It was written after Venezuelan independence and projects later conflicts back onto the colonial era
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The credit line dates the observations to 1800, before Venezuela's independence struggle began in 1810 and 1811.

options.text: It relies only on Indigenous oral traditions rather than on direct observation of the land
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt is built on Humboldt's own observations and natural science reasoning. It cites no Indigenous oral sources.

facts: Humboldt traveled in Spanish America from 1799 to 1804 as a foreign scientific visitor.
Venezuela declared independence in 1811.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line describes Humboldt as a traveling Prussian naturalist, and the text covers only physical environmental processes, not the experiences of workers.

items.stem: EXTRA: The growth of sugar, indigo, and cotton cultivation described in the excerpt depended heavily on which labor system?

options.text: Slavery of Africans and people of African descent on large estates
options.label: key
options.why: Plantations in colonial Venezuela, including the sugar estates of Aragua, depended heavily on enslaved people of African descent until slavery was abolished in 1854.

options.text: Indentured workers recruited from India and China after abolition in the British Caribbean
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Large-scale Asian indentured labor followed British abolition in the 1830s and was centered in British colonies, not in Spanish Venezuela around 1800.

options.text: The mita, a rotating labor draft imposed on Andean Indigenous communities for silver mining
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The mita supplied labor mainly to silver mines such as Potosí in the Andes, not to Venezuelan cash crop plantations.

options.text: Wage labor in mechanized mills organized into industrial unions
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Industrial unions grew up in later industrial economies. They did not exist on colonial Venezuelan plantations around 1800.

facts: Plantation agriculture in colonial Venezuela relied heavily on enslaved Africans and their descendants.
Venezuela abolished slavery in 1854; Britain abolished slavery in its colonies in 1833.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt names the plantation crops and the European planters but leaves the workforce unstated, so students must supply the labor system from what they know of the period.
design.evidence_quote: as they are everywhere in America by the European planters

items.stem: Which of the following best explains the historical situation in which Darwin made the observations described in the excerpt?

options.text: A British naval voyage was charting coasts and harbors to aid Britain's expanding seaborne trade.
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says the Beagle was surveying coasts and islands around the world. The Royal Navy's hydrographic surveys of the 1830s mapped coastlines and harbors to make navigation safer for British commerce and naval power.

options.text: Britain had sent officials to take formal control of the islands and organize a new settler colony there.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The excerpt says the colony was made up of exiles from the Republic of the Equator (Ecuador), which claimed the islands in 1832. It was not a British colony.

options.text: The Spanish crown was funding scientific expeditions to catalog the natural resources of its American colonies.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Spanish royal expeditions of this kind took place in the late 1700s. By 1835 Spain had lost its South American mainland colonies, and Darwin sailed on a British ship.

options.text: A missionary society was sending naturalists to accompany efforts to convert Pacific Islanders to Christianity.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Missionaries were active in the Pacific in this period, but the Beagle was a naval survey ship. The source says nothing about any missionary purpose.

facts: H.M.S. Beagle carried out a Royal Navy hydrographic survey, mainly of South American coasts, from 1831 to 1836.
Darwin sailed on the Beagle as a naturalist and visited the Galapagos in 1835.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says Darwin was aboard H.M.S. Beagle when it surveyed coasts and islands in 1831-1836.

items.stem: Which of the following claims does Darwin make about the human presence in the Galapagos Islands?

options.text: Seafarers had visited the islands for a long time, but permanent settlement was recent.
options.label: key
options.why: Darwin writes that buccaneers and then whalers had long visited the archipelago, but a small colony had existed only for the last six years.

options.text: The islands' inhabitants were descendants of an indigenous people who had lived there for centuries.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Darwin calls the inhabitants recent arrivals who had been banished from Ecuador. He does not mention any long-established native population.

options.text: British whaling companies had founded the colony to supply their crews with fresh food and water.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Darwin mentions whalers as visitors only. He says the colony was made up of people exiled from the Republic of the Equator.

options.text: The settlers had come voluntarily from Quito seeking farmland after the end of Spanish rule there.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Darwin says the settlers had been banished for political crimes, so they did not come voluntarily.

facts: Ecuador formally claimed the Galapagos Islands in 1832 and used them partly as a place of exile.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Darwin contrasts the long history of visits by buccaneers and whalers with a colony founded only six years earlier.
design.evidence_quote: long been frequented, first by the bucaniers, and latterly by whalers, but it is only within the last six years, that a small colony

items.stem: Darwin's reference to whalers frequenting the archipelago is best understood in the context of which nineteenth-century development?

options.text: Rising demand for whale oil for lamps and machine lubrication spurred long Pacific voyages.
options.label: key
options.why: In the early and mid-1800s, whale oil was used for lighting and for lubricating machinery in industrializing economies. This demand sent whaling fleets on long voyages into the Pacific, and island stops such as the Galapagos served those fleets.

options.text: The Manila galleon trade carried American silver across the Pacific to purchase Chinese silk and porcelain.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Manila galleon trade belonged to the period from 1565 to 1815. It moved silver, not whale products, and it had ended before Darwin's 1835 visit.

options.text: Steam-powered ships had replaced sailing vessels in long-distance Pacific commerce by the 1830s.
options.label: overstated
options.why: In the 1830s, steamships did not yet dominate long ocean routes. Whalers of this era were sailing ships.
