options.text: Plantation agriculture expanded on Pacific islands to grow sugar for export to industrial markets.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Sugar plantations did expand in places like Hawaii later in the century, but this does not explain why whalers visited the Galapagos.

facts: Nineteenth-century whale oil was widely used for lamp lighting and as a lubricant for machinery.
American and British whaling fleets hunted extensively in the Pacific in the early to mid-1800s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Darwin says that whalers had more recently been frequenting the archipelago.
design.evidence_quote: first by the bucaniers, and latterly by whalers

items.stem: Darwin's later theory of evolution by natural selection, informed by observations like those in the excerpt, was connected to which late nineteenth-century development?

options.text: Some writers adapted his ideas into Social Darwinism to justify imperial rule over other peoples.
options.label: key
options.why: After the theory appeared in On the Origin of Species (1859), some writers applied ideas of struggle and survival to human societies. These Social Darwinist arguments were used to justify imperialism and racial hierarchies in the late 1800s.

options.text: His theory supplied the scientific basis for Enlightenment arguments for natural rights and popular sovereignty.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Enlightenment arguments about natural rights date from the 1600s and 1700s, long before Darwin's 1859 theory.

options.text: His findings persuaded European governments to end their colonial expansion in Africa and Asia in the 1880s.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The 1880s saw a speeding up of European expansion, including the Scramble for Africa. Darwin-derived ideas were more often used to justify that expansion.

options.text: It was the main inspiration for the Marxist argument that class conflict drives historical change.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Marx and Engels set out their class-conflict theory in the Communist Manifesto (1848), before Darwin published his theory.

facts: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.
Social Darwinism was used in the late 1800s to justify imperialism and racial hierarchies.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt records Darwin's close observation of Galapagos tortoises and birds, the kind of evidence he later used in his theory.
design.evidence_quote: I met two large tortoises, each of which must have weighed at least two hundred pounds

items.stem: Darwin's reference to the Republic of the Equator, with its capital at Quito, reflects which development in the decades before his 1835 visit?

options.text: Wars of independence in the early 1800s ended Spanish rule over much of South America.
options.label: key
options.why: The Spanish American independence wars created new republics. Ecuador became independent in 1830 when it left Gran Colombia, and in 1832 it claimed the Galapagos.

options.text: The Haitian Revolution created the first independent state led by formerly enslaved people.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Haiti became independent in 1804, but that revolution in the Caribbean does not explain the existence of a republic based in Quito.

options.text: The Spanish-American War of 1898 stripped Spain of Cuba and Puerto Rico, its last colonies in the Americas.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Spanish-American War came more than sixty years after Darwin's visit, so it could not have shaped a republic that already existed in 1835.

options.text: Portugal's royal court fled to Brazil, which later became an independent empire under its own monarch.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Brazil's independence was a separate process in Portuguese America and is not connected to Ecuador's emergence.

facts: Ecuador separated from Gran Colombia and became an independent republic in 1830.
Most of Spanish South America gained independence in wars fought between about 1810 and 1825.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Darwin names the Republic of the Equator, with its capital at Quito, as the state that banished the settlers.
design.evidence_quote: the Republic of the Equator, of which Quito is the capital

items.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the excerpt as a source for historians studying the experiences of the Galapagos settlers in the 1830s?

options.text: Darwin, a brief visitor, summarizes the settlers without recording their own views.
options.label: key
options.why: Darwin was a passing British naturalist. He gives only a number, a racial description and the reason for exile, so the settlers' own experiences of banishment are absent.

options.text: Darwin had no firsthand experience of the islands and relied on reports from whalers.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt is a firsthand account. Darwin describes walking on the islands and meeting tortoises in person.

options.text: Darwin was an Ecuadorian official whose account defends the government's policy of exiling critics.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit line identifies Darwin as a British naturalist. He reports the exile without defending it.

options.text: The excerpt was written centuries after the settlement and depends on fading oral traditions.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Darwin wrote within a few years of his 1835 visit, and he says the colony was only six years old.

facts: Darwin visited the Galapagos for several weeks in 1835 as the Beagle's naturalist, not as a resident.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Darwin's only description of the inhabitants is their number, their color and the fact that they were banished, which shows an outsider's brief view.
design.evidence_quote: they are nearly all people of colour, who have been banished for political crimes
